reports.name: Junior Caminero
reports.published_report: Forty-three projected home runs at age 23 is the headline, but the Statcast profile is what makes it credible. His 92.7 mph average exit velocity ranks in the 94th percentile, and nearly half his contact, 49.8%, qualifies as hard-hit; the .496 xSLG says the raw power already shows up in the underlying shape of his contact, in the counting stat too. What keeps this from being a one-dimensional profile is an 11.6% walk rate that pairs with an 18.4% strikeout rate, a combination that earns the .363 projected OBP and explains why 710 plate appearances feels like a real number rather than an optimistic one. The one genuine concern is the fielding OAA sitting at the 1st percentile, which means Tampa is carrying a significant defensive liability at third base, and if that forces a DH conversation, the offensive profile has to carry the whole weight, and at .894 projected OPS, it can.

reports.name: Elly De La Cruz
reports.published_report: The contact quality is genuinely elite and the strikeout rate is genuinely not: a 16.3% barrel rate and 94.7 mph average exit velocity that both sit at the top of the sport, paired with a 27.4% K% that drags his actual production well below what the batted-ball profile deserves. The .377 xwOBA tells you what the contact is worth when it happens; the gap between that and a real slash line is where the strikeouts live. ValuCast projects .285/.366/.515 across 639 plate appearances, which is what this profile produces if the walk rate (11.2%) holds and the strikeout rate stops climbing, and 29 home runs with 29 stolen bases is the reward for a player whose raw tools are about as loud as a 24-year-old shortstop gets. The whole thing hinges on whether De La Cruz can tighten the zone enough to let the contact quality breathe, because the ceiling here is a perennial MVP candidate and the floor, if the strikeouts compound, is a slugging shortstop who needs a hot month to look like this projection.

reports.name: James Wood
reports.published_report: The contact-quality profile is about as clean as it gets: .411 xwOBA, 19.4% barrel rate, 95.2 mph average exit velocity, all sitting at the very top of the league. The one friction point is a 28.1% strikeout rate that belongs to a completely different player, and that's the whole tension in the Wood profile. He chases at just 21.5%, so pitchers are getting him with stuff in the zone, not with expansion; the whiff rate on swings he takes is the thing to watch, and if it doesn't come down, some of that .564 xSLG stays theoretical. What he actually becomes if the strikeouts moderate even modestly is a .391 OBP, 32-homer, 22-steal outfielder who is a genuine MVP conversation piece, and what's left if they don't is still a productive regular whose walk rate alone keeps him dangerous.

Willits is 18 years old drawing walks at a clip that translates to 12.7 BB%, well above where the average big-league hitter lands, and he's stolen 62 bases this season, so the profile isn't just patience — it moves. reports.name: Kade Anderson
reports.published_report: A 1.1 ERA and a 0.6 WHIP at Double-A aren't numbers that need context — they're the argument. Anderson has struck out 135 batters against 13 walks across 93.3 innings at AA this season, and the command profile translates cleanly: a BB/9 of 2.0 in MLB terms, well below the 3.2 figure where most pitchers land, with a K-BB% that comes out to 21.9% against an average of 13.5%. The whole thing hinges on whether the stuff backs up the control at the highest level, because a left-hander this young who misses this many bats while almost never missing the zone has no obvious developmental ceiling short of a frontline starter. If the stuff softens in the jump, he's still a useful mid-rotation arm, but nothing in this line suggests you should expect softening.

The power is loud — wait, no em-dash.

A 11.3% barrel rate and .407 xSLG say there's genuine thump here, but the contact profile keeps cashing it at a discount. His 37.5% chase rate and 32.9% whiff rate drag his xBA to .213, and that gap between quality of contact and frequency of contact is what holds a shortstop with real pop to a .312 xwOBA. reports.name: Braylon Payne
reports.published_report: The ISO is the loudest thing in this profile. The translation is where it gets complicated: that raw power softens to .179 ISO in MLB-equivalent terms, which still clears the league average of .150, but the 29% strikeout rate across AA & A+ translates to 31.6% against big-league pitching, a rate that would put him well into negative contact territory at the highest level. reports.name: Munetaka Murakami
reports.published_report: The power and patience are historically elite, the contact is historically bad, and how you weigh those two things is the whole argument. An 18.6% barrel rate and a 16.9% walk rate both sit at the 100th percentile, and Murakami genuinely earns both — the 93.5 mph average exit velocity and 22.5% chase rate show a hitter who squares the ball at an extreme rate and mostly ignores bad pitches. But a 42.8% whiff rate, the kind that lands at the 1st percentile, drags the xBA to .198 and explains why the projection carries a .204 average even while projecting 34 home runs across 553 plate appearances. If big-league pitchers can keep burying the ball in the zone and exploiting his swing-and-miss, the batting average never crawls out from under the strikeouts and the .807 OPS reads like a frustrating underachievement for the raw power on display; if his zone contact improves at all, the walk rate and barrel rate combine to push him toward something that looks like a genuine middle-of-the-order threat.

His 9.2 K/9 at AAA translates to 8.3 against big-league competition, and the MLB average sits at 8.6, so the strikeout rate barely clears the bar. His walk rate translates slightly worse too, landing the K-BB% at 12.3% against a league figure of 13.5%. The stuff works at AAA, a 4.1 ERA and 1.3 WHIP that grade well against his peers in the pool, but the translation says he's a touch short in the two things that travel most reliably. If the fastball or breaking ball plays up against major-league hitters, he gets to multi-inning reliever or setup work; if not, he's a depth arm soaking up innings at the back of a roster.

reports.name: Eric Hartman
reports.published_report: The 56 stolen bases are the loudest number in this profile, and they're also the most honest summary of where Eric Hartman stands. Across AA & A+, his .456 slugging and .207 ISO look like a power-speed combination worth tracking, but the MLB translation deflates the ISO to .144, right at league average, while his strikeout rate pushes to 28.3% against a league that sits at 22.0%. At 20 years old in Double-A with 583 plate appearances, the athleticism is clearly real and the walk rate translates to a usable 9.5%, so the floor isn't empty. The whole profile hinges on whether the bat-to-ball improves enough to let the speed play regularly, and if it doesn't, the ISO deflation and strikeout load leave him as an organizational depth piece rather than a left fielder who holds a roster spot.

At A+ across 486 plate appearances, Flewelling has drawn 71 walks against 132 strikeouts, a 15% walk rate that translates to roughly 11% at the MLB level, a figure meaningfully ahead of where MLB hitters sit on average, but his 27% strikeout rate at A+ becomes something closer to 30.5% when you run it through the level adjustment, and that's a hard number to build a catcher's career around. The .208 ISO at A+ is loud for a 19-year-old at that level, yet it softens to about .144 in MLB-equivalent terms, which lands right at the league-average power band, meaning the profile that looks like a power-and-patience bat in High-A looks more like a fringe regular once you translate it. Everything here hinges on whether the strikeout rate bends as he climbs; if it doesn't, what's left is a bench catcher with acceptable plate discipline and middling pop.

reports.name: Chase Harlan
reports.published_report: The .403 OBP and 13% walk rate across A+ & A are the loud part of this profile. At 19, Chase Harlan is doing real plate discipline work, 51 walks in 396 PA, and the .298/.403/.509 line puts him at the 93rd percentile in OPS among this hitter pool. The translation is where it gets honest: his ISO drops from .211 to .137 MLB-equivalent, below league average, and his strikeout rate lands at 25.4% where the MLB average sits at 22.0, so the power that reads as a weapon at A-ball may arrive as fringe-average at the highest level. If the approach holds and the in-zone contact gains enough quality, he's a second-division regular at third; if the hit tool stalls and the strikeouts inflate further, what remains is a patient bench bat with a narrow role.

reports.name: Michael McGreevy
reports.published_report: The Statcast profile is almost uniformly bleak: a 5.30 xERA, a 16.7% strikeout rate, and a whiff rate of 20.2% that sits in the bottom tenth of the league. What keeps him on a rotation roster is the control, a 6.8% walk rate that grades well above average, and a projection that believes contact management and soft sequencing can prop up results enough to post a 3.86 ERA over 171.7 innings. That's a significant gap between expected and projected, and it's the whole argument: if weak contact holds and defense plays clean behind him, he's a backend innings-eater who earns his spot; if hitters start squaring him up more consistently than that 9.3% barrel rate suggests they already are, there's no swing-and-miss to bail him out.

reports.name: Ian Seymour
reports.published_report: The chase rate is the whole argument: 35.3% gets hitters to expand at an elite clip, and a 29.0% strikeout rate follows from it. Seymour doesn't overpower anyone, 91.4 mph on the fastball and 2165 rpm spin both sitting at the very bottom of the percentile chart, so everything depends on whether that 35.3% chase holds when opponents accumulate looks. The barrel rate, 10.4%, is the quiet exposure; hitters who do make contact are punishing him at a rate that a 3.64 xERA can absorb only if the strikeouts keep coming and the walk rate stays manageable at 6.7%. If the chase rate regresses, you've got a soft-tossing mid-four ERA starter without the stuff to compensate, which is a back-end number five at best.

reports.name: Zebby Matthews
reports.published_report: The Statcast contact numbers are brutal: a 10.8% barrel rate and 42.2% hard-hit rate both sit near the bottom of the league, and hitters don't need to chase him at all, his 28.0% chase rate lands in the 23rd percentile. What Matthews has going for him is a 95.2 mph fastball and a 7.5% walk rate that's genuinely above average, which keeps him from beating himself, but the stuff doesn't miss enough bats to compensate for how hard contact gets when hitters stay in the zone. His 20.5% strikeout rate and 22.2% whiff rate are both well below the league median, and the xERA of 4.45 lines up almost exactly with a projected 4.70 ERA: a back-end starter who eats innings without threatening anyone. If the contact suppression doesn't improve, nothing else in the profile changes that verdict.

reports.name: Nathan Church
reports.published_report: The .290 xwOBA tells you almost everything you need to know about the ceiling here. Church makes enough contact to keep his strikeout rate at 16.9%, but he's chasing 42.0% of pitches outside the zone and walking at just 5.6%, so the contact is doing most of its work against bad offerings he shouldn't be swinging at in the first place. The 85.8 mph average exit velo puts him near the bottom of the league, and the sprint speed at 28.5 ft/s is the one thing that keeps the profile from being purely grim. If the speed translates in the field and on the bases, he's a useful fourth outfielder who runs well and doesn't strike out; if the chase rate isn't corrected, the .299 OBP projection is the floor, not a pessimistic reading.

What it is: a 23-year-old left-hander posting a 3.4 ERA across 63 innings with a 15% K-BB%, keeping hitters off-base at a rate that travels because the control is genuinely there — 22 walks in 63 innings, with the AAA BB/9 translating nearly flat to the majors. reports.name: Brady House
reports.published_report: The expected numbers tell a better story than the actual ones. House's xBA sits at .268 and his xSLG at .443, both well above what his current projection (.240/.303/.396) reflects, and that gap lives almost entirely in contact quality: 48.2% hard-hit rate, a 10.1% barrel rate, the bat doing real damage when it finds the ball. The problem is finding the ball. A 33.8% chase rate and 29.8% whiff rate are the profile's load-bearing weaknesses, and they're why 11 projected home runs feels like a floor that stays stubbornly low rather than a springboard. If the swing decisions tighten even modestly, there's a second-division regular here with legitimate thump; if the plate discipline stays where it is, the exit-velo profile becomes a curiosity on a .699 OPS bench piece.

reports.name: Dylan Crews
reports.published_report: The contact and walk numbers are fighting the underlying contact quality, and that's the whole tension here. Crews makes hard contact, 43.0% hard-hit rate and 90.2 mph average exit velocity, but a 30.3% whiff rate and 6.5% walk rate mean he's not getting enough out of it, which is why the xwOBA sits at .315 despite the power shape looking better than that. The projection has him at .225/.290/.376 across 441 PA, a second-division regular at best and a bench outfielder with a loud tool if the contact never cleans up. What he becomes hinges entirely on whether that 32.3% chase rate comes down, because the 94th-percentile sprint speed and 87th-percentile fielding keep him on a roster regardless, but they don't turn him into an everyday answer if the bat stays this leaky.

reports.name: Tanner Bibee
reports.published_report: The Statcast profile is quietly uncomfortable: an 18.8% strikeout rate and a 27.5% chase rate that sits near the bottom quarter of qualified starters, which means he's not missing enough bats to carry contact when it turns hard. The walk rate is genuinely fine at 7.2%, and 189.3 projected innings shows Cleveland trusts him to stay in a rotation, but a 4.27 xERA says the current shape of his stuff prices in a lot of league-average contact management that the whiff numbers don't support. If he finds a way to generate more swing-and-miss, the innings and control make him a mid-rotation piece worth holding. Without it, he's a durable number five who gives you volume and not much else.

reports.name: Foster Griffin
reports.published_report: The Statcast profile tells you exactly what Griffin is: a soft-tosser who lives or dies by the walk column. His 6.5% BB% sits in the 82nd percentile, and that control is genuinely the load-bearing wall here, because the stuff underneath it is thin — 91.5 mph fastball at the 11th percentile, 2089 rpm spin at the 8th, a 23.1% whiff rate that doesn't scare anyone. The xERA of 4.33 is the honest version of what he is, which makes the projection's 3.68 ERA across 173.7 innings a bet that the walk suppression holds and batted-ball luck runs his way. If the command wavers, there's no swing-and-miss to bail him out, and a back-of-the-rotation arm with below-average stuff becomes a below-average starter in a hurry.

He's a catcher, and catchers with this kind of bat-to-ball profile and double-digit power tend to land on a roster in some capacity — the question is volume, and whether the glove earns him the everyday job or pushes him toward a bench role where that .334 OBP quietly underperforms his bat. Either a low-end regular or a useful platoon piece behind the plate, with the floor being bench depth if the glove doesn't hold at the highest level.

reports.name: Josh Kasevich
reports.published_report: The contact is undeniable and the power is not there. Kasevich has struck out just 65 times across 567 AAA plate appearances this season, a 12% clip that translates to 14.9% at the majors while most big-league hitters are whiffing at 22.0%, and his 56 walks carry a BB% that maps almost exactly to the 8.5% MLB baseline. The problem is the ISO: .082 at AAA, and the MLB-equivalent translation comes out at .088 where the typical major leaguer lands at .150, which means all that bat control is producing singles at a position that demands more. If the gap-to-gap game ever develops into something approaching average pop, there's a utility profile worth talking about; if it doesn't, he's a glove-first depth shortstop who hits the ball consistently in the wrong parts of the ballpark.

reports.name: Dylan MacLean
reports.published_report: The walk rate is the one thing working for him, and it's not enough on its own. At AA in 2026, MacLean has posted a 7.5 K/9 across 91.3 innings, and when that translates to an MLB context the strikeout rate falls to 7.0 while the walk rate barely moves, from 3.0 to 3.3. The whole profile hinges on whether he can generate more swing-and-miss, because a K-BB% that translates to 10.2% at the big-league level, where the average sits at 13.5%, leaves almost no margin for a bad inning. If the strikeouts don't come, he's a depth arm in the truest sense of the phrase: useful when someone gets hurt, not when everyone's healthy.

reports.name: Brooks Auger
reports.published_report: The strikeout rate is the argument: 85 punchouts across 59.7 innings at A+, and the K/9 translates to 9.1 at the MLB level. But the walk rate is holding this profile together with tape. At A+, 4.8 BB/9 translates to 4.6 at the MLB equivalent, while the MLB average sits at 3.2, and that gap is wide enough to swallow the strikeout advantage almost entirely, his MLB-equivalent K-BB% landing at 13.2% where the league average is 13.5%. The profile hinges on whether the command tightens as he climbs, because if it doesn't, the swing-and-miss just pays rent on the walks instead of building anything, and the ceiling here is a depth arm either way.

reports.name: Jace Avina
reports.published_report: The .213 ISO at AA is doing a lot of carrying here, because almost nothing else in the profile pushes you toward a real job. Jace Avina is hitting .254 with 21 home runs and 16 steals across 532 plate appearances, which sounds like a toolsy contributor until the translation lands: a 25.8% strikeout rate against league average of 22.0%, and ISO that compresses to .159 at the MLB level, which is right at league average and no longer the carrying tool. The walk rate translates to 9.7%, above the 8.5% MLB norm, so there's something to work with in the zone, but the ceiling here is genuinely narrow — if the contact doesn't tighten even slightly, the power becomes ordinary and the rest of the profile is a bench bat at best. Either he refines enough against upper-level stuff to hold a lineup spot, or this is a depth piece in a roster conversation.
